original_question: For the finite interval n = {0, 1, ..., n-1} with counting measure and integer central symmetries, let bms_r(n) be the blurred maximal symmetry number obtained by taking the infimum over measurable blurred r-colorings. Calculate the values of bms_r(n), at least for small n and for r = 2.
target_in_paper: Section 6, Problem 6.3: "Calculate the values bms_r(n) (at least for small n and r = 2)."
correct_elements: Your draft correctly targets the paper's discrete blurred-symmetry problem rather than the interval problem: it uses the finite ordinal n={0,1,...,n-1}, the counting-measure setting, the central-symmetry framework on the integers, the quantity bms_r(n), and the paper's stated interest in small n and the two-color case.
missing_details: The exact target in the paper is Problem 6.3 in Section 6; Problem 6.4 is a different question about ms_r(I) for the unit interval I=[0,1].

The ambient symmetry model should be stated exactly: n={0,1,...,n-1} is treated as a subset of Z with admissible symmetries s_c(x)=c-x for c in Z. Equivalently, the symmetry center is c/2, so half-integer centers are allowed.
A blurred r-coloring must be defined explicitly as a family (chi_1,...,chi_r) of functions chi_i:n->[0,1] such that chi_1(x)+...+chi_r(x)=1 for every x in n.

The infimum defining bms_r(n) needs its objective function, not just the phrase 'taking the infimum over blurred colorings'. After extending each chi_i by 0 outside n, one minimizes sup_{1<=i<=r} sup_{c in Z} sum_{x in Z} chi_i(x)chi_i(c-x), equivalently sup_{1<=i<=r} sup_{c in Z} sum_{x in n intersection (c-n)} chi_i(x)chi_i(c-x).
The quantifiers n,r in N should be stated explicitly.
On the finite set n, every subset is measurable, so the word 'measurable' is vacuous unless that is said explicitly.
To match the paper, the request should ask for exact values, at least in the cases of small n and in the two-color case r=2, rather than just estimates or asymptotics.

The nearby motivation from Theorem 6.2 is implicit in your draft: bms_r(I)=lim_{n->infinity} bms_r(n)/n, and for r>1 one has bms_r(I)=ms_r(I), which is why the finite discrete problem is singled out in Section 6.
refined_question: For integers n,r>=1, let n={0,1,...,n-1} be viewed as a subset of Z with counting measure and with admissible central symmetries s_c(x)=c-x for c in Z. A blurred r-coloring of n is a family chi=(chi_1,...,chi_r) of functions chi_i:n->[0,1] such that sum_{i=1}^r chi_i(x)=1 for every x in n. Extending each chi_i by 0 outside n, define the blurred maximal symmetry number by bms_r(n)=inf_chi sup_{1<=i<=r} sup_{c in Z} sum_{x in Z} chi_i(x)chi_i(c-x). Calculate the exact values of bms_r(n), at least in the cases of small n and, in particular, for the two-color case r=2.
justification: The draft is closest to Problem 6.3, not Problem 6.4, because it asks about the discrete blurred quantity bms_r(n) rather than the interval quantity ms_r(I). In Section 6, Banakh first introduces ms_r(I) for the unit interval and the related discrete numbers ms_r(n) for finite ordinals n as subsets of Z with symmetries x->c-x; he then defines blurred colorings and the blurred maximal symmetry number bms_r(X); finally he states Problem 6.3 exactly for bms_r(n). Theorem 6.2 gives the nearby structural reason this finite problem matters: bms_r(I)=lim_{n->infinity} bms_r(n)/n, and for r>1, bms_r(I)=ms_r(I).
